passage: Rosa was closing the shop in Toronto when Tariq, her coworker, stayed behind and said quietly that he hadn't been sleeping and that lately everything felt too heavy to carry. Rosa put the keys down and sat. She didn't offer quick fixes or tell him to cheer up. "That sounds really hard," she said. "Do you want to tell me more, or just sit for a bit?" He talked for ten minutes, then said, "Please don't tell anyone." Rosa answered slowly, "I won't gossip about this. But if I ever think you're not safe, I would want to get you help, and I'd tell you first." He nodded. Before leaving she asked if he'd thought about seeing a doctor or a counsellor, and offered to sit with him while he looked up the clinic's hours.

qa.q: Where was Rosa when Tariq spoke to her?
qa.a: She was closing the shop in Toronto.

qa.q: What was Tariq worried about when he said "Please don't tell anyone"?
qa.a: He was probably worried about being judged or exposed, though he may also have wanted to keep some control over his story.

qa.q: What did Rosa do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: She listened without fixing, was clear about the limit of confidentiality and offered to help him find a doctor or counsellor; next she could check in gently.

qa.q: How might Rosa have felt when Tariq asked her not to tell anyone?
qa.a: Rosa was probably torn and concerned, wanting to keep his trust but also keep him safe, which is why she answered slowly and set a limit. 🤍

grounding: A young adult listens to a confidence without judgment, does not rush to fix or share it, and encourages professional help while being clear that safety limits confidentiality.

passage: The community centre's back room was empty after the evening classes. Darshan, a fellow volunteer, was folding chairs when he said, half to the floor, "I've been having panic attacks before my exams. I haven't told anyone." Urmila stopped stacking. She didn't say "Don't worry" or start listing tips. "That sounds frightening. Is it more a racing heart, or a dread that builds?" she asked, and he said the dread. "I'm glad you told me," she said. "I won't repeat it. Would it help to talk to someone trained for this? The centre has a counsellor on Saturdays." Darshan shrugged, then said he might. He stacked the last chair. Urmila noticed he looked lighter, and wondered if she had said the right things at all.

qa.q: When does the centre's counsellor come?
qa.a: On Saturdays.

qa.q: What was Urmila worried about at the end of the scene?
qa.a: She wondered whether she had said the right things at all, even though Darshan looked lighter.

qa.q: What could Urmila do if Darshan does not go to the counsellor?
qa.a: She can keep listening without pushing, and gently check in later, leaving the choice of help to him.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Darshan to say it aloud?
qa.a: It may have felt frightening and like a relief at once, as his half-spoken words and looking lighter afterwards suggest.

grounding: A young adult receiving a confidence listens without judgment, does not share it, and encourages qualified help.

passage:
Dear Gurpreet,
Thank you for trusting me on Saturday. I've thought about what you said all weekend, and I wanted to write rather than text.
First: I haven't told anyone, and I won't. What you shared about feeling flat and not wanting to get out of bed some mornings is yours to share when you choose.
Second: I'm sorry I jumped in with advice so quickly. You didn't ask me to fix it, and I heard myself listing solutions while you were still talking. Next time I'll listen first.
Third, gently: I think a counsellor could help more than I can. The one my cousin sees in Ludhiana is kind and doesn't rush. I'd be happy to come with you to the first appointment, or just sit outside.
And one honest thing: if you ever felt unsafe, or thought about hurting yourself, I would need to get you help, even if that meant telling someone. I hope you'd understand why.
With love,
Jyoti

qa.q: When did Gurpreet confide in Jyoti?
qa.a: On Saturday.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel about having jumped in with advice?
qa.a: Jyoti feels sorry and a little regretful for listing solutions while Gurpreet was still talking.

qa.q: What does Jyoti offer, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Jyoti keeps the confidence, offers to go with Gurpreet to a counsellor, and is honest that safety would come before secrecy, which is supportive and clear.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel reassured and cared for, knowing the confidence is kept and help is offered without pressure.

grounding: Shows a young adult honouring a friend's confidence, regretting rushing to fix, encouraging professional help and naming the safety limit of secrecy.

passage: Bhavna, you asked why I believe some secrets can't be kept. Last year, in the working women's hostel in Pune, my roommate Ritu told me something at midnight. She'd been hurting herself, and she'd been thinking she'd be better off not here. Then she said, "Promise you won't tell anyone." I didn't promise. I sat on her bed, held her hand and said, "Thank you for telling me. You're not a burden. And I care too much to keep this to myself tonight." She cried. I stayed right beside her and called the warden, Mrs. Gomes, from my phone. She came up in five minutes, sat with us, and called the crisis helpline with Ritu on speaker. By morning Ritu had an appointment with a counsellor, and her sister was on the way from Nashik. Ritu was angry with me for a week. Then she said thank you. So, from me, Trisha: listen without judging. But when someone's at risk, you get help that same night.

qa.q: Where was the working women's hostel?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when she asked Trisha to promise not to tell?
qa.a: Ritu was likely frightened and ashamed, afraid of being judged or exposed, even as she reached out.

qa.q: Why was Trisha right not to keep the secret that night?
qa.a: Ritu was at risk, so Trisha stayed with her, reassured her, and called the warden, who got the crisis helpline on the line that same night.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Gomes respond when Trisha called?
qa.a: She came up within five minutes, sat with them, and called the crisis helpline with Ritu on speaker.

grounding: Shows a young adult listening to a friend's disclosure without judgment and recognising that risk to safety means getting help the same night.

passage: I'm Sachin, and my desk is next to the small meeting room where Hafsa, our team lead, sometimes takes calls. On Tuesday the new intern, Zoya, went in with her, and through the glass I could see Zoya crying. I didn't hear everything. I heard Zoya say, "Please don't tell anyone," and Hafsa say gently, "I'll listen to all of it first." Hafsa sat forward and didn't interrupt for a long time. Then I caught part of her answer: "...not your fault. Because it involves a senior touching you, I can't keep this only between us. I have to take it to the Internal Committee today. I'll come with you, and I'll tell you every step." Zoya nodded slowly. An hour later I saw them walk to the committee chair's office together. By evening, the manager in question had been told not to contact Zoya while the complaint was reviewed. I still don't know the details, and that's right.

qa.q: Which body did Hafsa say she had to take it to?
qa.a: The Internal Committee.

qa.q: What might Zoya have been feeling when she said 'Please don't tell anyone'?
qa.a: Zoya was likely scared and ashamed, worried about what would happen if others knew, even as she sought help.

qa.q: How did Hafsa handle the disclosure well?
qa.a: She listened fully without rushing, said it wasn't Zoya's fault, explained honestly why she couldn't keep it secret, and went with Zoya to the committee that day.

qa.q: How does Sachin see his own role?
qa.a: Sachin noticed enough to understand something serious had happened, but feels it's right not to know the details, respecting Zoya's privacy.

grounding: An observer describes a young team lead listening to a disclosure without judgment and explaining that harm means it must go to the committee that day.

passage:
Tuesday, first week. Over tea in the canteen, Arnab told Pallavi he had lost his job and hadn't told his family. "Please keep it to yourself." She listened, didn't offer to fix his CV, didn't tell anyone. "Thank you for trusting me," she said.
Monday, the week after. Arnab called late, voice flat. He hadn't eaten properly in days. Then: "Honestly, nobody would notice if I just disappeared."
Pallavi's stomach went cold. "Arnab, I'm really glad you told me. I'm worried about your safety, and this is one thing I can't keep secret." She stayed on the line, called a helpline with him on speaker, and then, with his okay, rang his elder brother, who drove over that same night.
Saturday, two weeks later. Arnab met her outside the counsellor's clinic. "You broke my secret," he said, and then, "I'm glad you did."

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Pallavi in the canteen?
qa.a: He asked, "Please keep it to yourself."

qa.q: What did Pallavi feel when Arnab said nobody would notice if he disappeared?
qa.a: Pallavi felt alarmed and frightened for his safety; her stomach went cold.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that night, and why was it right?
qa.a: She told Arnab she couldn't keep this secret, stayed on the line, called a helpline with him and rang his elder brother, because his safety mattered more than confidentiality.

qa.q: How did Arnab come to see the broken secret?
qa.a: At first he felt his trust had been broken, but two weeks later, outside the counsellor's clinic, he said he was glad she did it.

grounding: A young adult receiving a confidence listens without judging or fixing, keeps it private, but breaks confidentiality the same night when the friend's safety is at risk.
